testCases.name: test_case_0
testCases.input: Compare guardrails vs app logic: why separate, testable, pluggable wrappers instead of hardcoding?
testCases.actualOutput:
- Keep guardrails separate because they are cross-cutting concerns (like logging or auth). They apply across many components (input, retriever, generator) so hardcoding them everywhere causes duplication and risk of missing or breaking code.

- Make them testable independently because you must verify the rules work on their own. You do not test them only through the app; you validate the guardrails layer separately to be sure the rules behave correctly.

- Make them pluggable and composable (wrappers) so you can add, remove, reorder, or replace rules without changing app logic. That lets you change guardrails by editing the guardrails layer only, avoiding rewrites of the application.

- Use a guard object that attaches validators (individual guardrails). Validators are the single rules (e.g., “no toxic output”) that work across different app types (RAG, agents, chatbots) because guardrails act on a contract, not implementation details.

- Keep guardrails after evaluation and observability because you iterate and improve the app during evaluation. If you hardcode guardrails too early you’d have to re-implement them each iteration. Observability helps you inspect input→output; guardrails are like a wrapper you apply afterward (they don’t change how you open the box, just wrap it).

- The father–son analogy: guardrails and the app are related but separate identities — independent so you can manage and evolve each without coupling them.
testCases.expectedOutput:
Guardrails should be separate from app logic because they are **cross-cutting concerns** like logging or authorization: they apply across many parts of the app, not just one place.

Keeping them as a **wrapper/layer** instead of hardcoding them gives these benefits:
- **Avoids breaking app code** when guardrails change
- **Prevents missed enforcement** across input, retriever, generator, etc.
- **Makes guardrails independently testable**
- **Keeps them pluggable and composable** so you can add, remove, or reorder validators without rewriting the app
- **Lets you improve or evaluate guardrails separately** from the application

In short, app logic handles the core workflow, while guardrails validate it against rules/specs as a separate, reusable layer.

testCases.name: test_case_4
testCases.input: Compare MLOps and LLMOps: models, workflows, and operational differences.
testCases.actualOutput:
Models
- ML models (traditional deep learning/ML): treated as deterministic to some extent — for a given input they generally give the same output. You train, evaluate and version these models as part of your pipeline.
- LLMs: probabilistic in nature — the same prompt/input can produce different outputs. In LLM Ops you often don’t train the core model from scratch (you typically already have a model); instead you build operations around using and adapting that model.

Workflows
- ML Ops: prediction is usually a direct input→model→output flow. The main pipelines you manage are the data pipeline and the model pipeline (training, evaluation, versioning). You don’t typically have a long multi-step runtime workflow for a single prediction.
- LLM Ops: LLM-based applications use explicit, possibly complex runtime workflows around the LLM. The workflow can vary in length and number of steps (prompting, chaining, retrieval, tool calls, post-processing). Because of this, you need to manage the full workflow, not just the model invocation.

Operational differences
- Focus: ML Ops centers on training, evaluating, versioning and deploying models you build. LLM Ops centers on the LLM in the middle of an application and the surrounding operations (tools, prompts, retrieval, adapters).
- Dynamics: LLM Ops is more dynamic — workflows change in complexity and behavior and outputs are probabilistic — so operational criteria and controls must adapt. ML Ops is complex but generally less dynamic at inference time.
- Scope: LLM Ops includes things like data preprocessing, language-model fine-tuning, monitoring, deployment, and other methods/tools/processes to use LLMs reliably across their lifecycle. (Oracle: LLM Ops = methods, tools and processes to use LLMs reliably.)
- Tracking & observability: Because LLM applications are workflow-driven and outputs vary, you need to track more of the end-to-end journey and workflow behavior than in typical ML prediction pipelines.
- Tooling claims: Some LLM Ops platform definitions emphasize things like library management and lower ops cost (enabling less technical personnel), but that description is of limited usefulness without focusing on workflow, monitoring and reliability.
testCases.expectedOutput:
MLOps and LLMOps differ mainly in what they operate on and how dynamic the workflow is.

- **MLOps** is centered around a **trained machine learning model**. You start with a dataset, use **input features** and a **target feature**, train the model, evaluate it, and manage versioning and deployment. The workflow is more fixed and less dynamic.
- **LLMOps** is centered around **LLM-based applications**. The model is usually already available, and the main task is to build a **workflow or application around it**. This workflow can vary in length and complexity, so the operational needs also change.
- In **MLOps**, the core focus is **model training, evaluation, and productionizing the model**.
- In **LLMOps**, the core focus is **orchestrating the application workflow around the model**, which is much more dynamic.

So, in short: **MLOps manages model-centric systems; LLMOps manages application/workflow-centric systems built on top of existing LLMs.**

testCases.actualOutput:
- NOOP: do nothing to the content. The input that triggered "PII detected" is returned unchanged, but the failure is recorded in Guardrails’ history/logs.

- Error logging: the failure is explicitly stored/logged (kept in Guardrails’ history). Like NOOP, it does not change the output; its purpose is monitoring/audit of the validation event.

- Auto-fix (redactic text): the validator applies a fix for the PII (e.g., redact or remove the sensitive text). The output is the modified/fixed content rather than the original.

testCases.name: test_case_8
testCases.input: How does the fact-extraction LLM differ from judge LLM, and when is each used?
testCases.actualOutput:
The fact-extraction LLM:
- Used first. It reads the expected output (answer key) or retrieved context and decomposes it into individual facts/claims (e.g., 20 or 5 fact units).
- It only extracts facts based on a prompt; it does not compare or judge anything.
- Its output is a list of fact units to be checked later.

The judge LLM:
- Used after extraction. It takes each fact unit plus the original query and decides whether that fact is relevant to the question (i.e., whether the answer is hidden in that fact).
- It acts as a verification system to evaluate another LLM’s response (e.g., a RAG output), reports relevance, gives a score, and explains the reason for the score.
- It runs over the extracted facts (e.g., in a loop) to compute overall contextual relevance (for example, 15 of 20 relevant).

In short: extraction LLM = produce fact units; judge LLM = compare those facts to the query and provide relevance judgments, scores, and reasons.
testCases.expectedOutput:
The **fact-extraction LLM** is used first to **break the expected answer into individual claims or facts**. It does **not compare** anything yet.

The **judge LLM** is used later to **compare those extracted claims against the retrieved context** and decide whether each claim is **supported/attributable** by the retriever’s output.

So:
- **Fact-extraction LLM** = extracts claims from the expected output
- **Judge LLM** = checks whether those claims appear in the retrieved context and evaluates recall/coverage

testCases.input: LLM vs human eval-data generation: speed, cost, scalability, reproducibility?
testCases.actualOutput:
Speed
- Human: slow — creating and annotating datasets by humans is time consuming.
- LLM: fast — LLMs can generate datasets quickly via a pipeline/workflow.

Cost
- Human: costly — human annotation and detailed judgment are expensive.
- LLM: cheaper — automated LLM generation costs less than humans.

Scalability
- Human: not scalable — human annotation does not scale for repeated/frequent evaluation.
- LLM: scalable — LLM-generated datasets can be produced at scale.

Reproducibility
- Human: low — hard to reproduce large-scale human labeling reliably and cheaply.
- LLM: higher — using a controlled pipeline/workflow lets you reproduce dataset generation across iterations.
  Caveat from context: LLM outputs are probabilistic and non-deterministic, so you must design the workflow (and controls like prompts, seeds, or verification steps) to achieve practical reproducibility.

Trade-off note
- Humans give better judgment and detailed reports (needed for text evaluation) but at high cost and low scale. LLMs give speed, lower cost, and scalability but need proper workflows and checks because outputs are semantically flexible and non-deterministic.

testCases.name: test_case_12
testCases.input: Langfuse getPrompt: label-based vs version-based prompt retrieval?
testCases.actualOutput:
Label-based (recommended)
- You request the prompt by name + label (examples: latest or baseline) and type (e.g., text).
- Labels are tags that point to a version. "latest" automatically resolves to the newest version, so you don't need to change code when you update the prompt.
- Use "baseline" to lock to a tagged baseline version without hard-coding a number.
- When you pull by label you get the prompt content and its version/metadata; you can compare configs across versions to see what changed.

Version-based (not recommended)
- You request the prompt by a specific version number.
- This requires hard-coding the version in your app; when you update the prompt you must change code and redeploy.
- Because of the redeployment/hard-coding issue, version-based selection is discouraged.

Practical note (from context)
- With langfuse.getprompt you only need to pass name, type, and label to pull the prompt (so using label "latest" avoids managing version numbers).

This way, Langfuse will automatically pull the latest version when the label points to a newer prompt, so you don’t need to update code every time the version changes.

testCases.name: test_case_14
testCases.input: How do generation, filtration, and evolution turn synthetic goldens into realistic QA pairs, and why style output?
testCases.actualOutput:
- Generation: create initial synthetic “goldens” (raw QA pairs). These are the first, automatically generated examples.

- Filtration: use a critique model (evaluator) and a threshold (default ~0.5, can be tuned — in the example set to 0.6) to score those goldens and remove the bad ones. Filtration drops questions that don’t meet the generation standards or that you couldn’t safely return from an LLM. This step ensures the remaining set is higher quality before further work.

- Evolution: take the filtered goldens (not the raw ones) and rewrite them with an LLM one or more times (num_evolution_times) to increase complexity and realism. Evolution makes synthetic examples more like human-curated QAs — more interesting, harder, and more realistic — so they better test real-world applications. The goal is to approach human quality (e.g., 80–90% of the way), accepting a scalability/quality trade-off.

- Styling: apply a consistent style to the input and output formats of the evolved goldens (configured in the evolution config). Styling makes examples uniform and realistic for downstream use (readability, format expectations, and easier evaluation).

In short: generate many raw examples, filter out low-quality ones with a critique model and threshold, then evolve the survivors into more complex, realistic QA pairs and style their format for consistent, usable output.

Evolution then makes the filtered questions more complex and realistic so they better test real-world applications. Styling is used to format the input and output of the evolved synthetic goldens.

- Complete Pinecone architecture and design.
- How to perform CRUD operations on the vector DB (collections, entries).
- How embeddings are created and retrieved.
- Internal algorithms for fast, low-latency retrieval.
- Hands-on testing: retrieving your details, collection name, unique file count, file names.

- Pinecone has LangChain (noted as “line chain”) integration built-in.
- Integration is very simple: create a Pinecone account, get an API key, and change 2–3 lines of code in your LangChain app to use Pinecone as the vector store.
- The instructor already discussed Pinecone code and will demo it in class so you can plug it into your application easily.

testCases.name: test_case_16
testCases.input: What is faithfulness, and how is its score computed from grounded/total claims?
testCases.actualOutput:
Faithfulness measures how much of a model’s response is grounded in the retrieved context (the ultimate truth) rather than coming from the model’s own parametric knowledge.

How the score is computed:
- Extract all factual claims from the model’s response (this set is the denominator — total claims).
- For each claim, compare against the retrieved context and label:  
  - "yes" (grounded) if the claim comes from the context,  
  - "no" if it contradicts or isn’t supported (hallucination),  
  - "I don't know" if it’s ambiguous / cannot be verified.
- A claim is considered truthful if it does not contradict any facts in the retrieval context.
- Faithfulness score = (number of grounded claims) / (total number of claims you counted in the denominator).

Example: If there are 10 extracted claims and 8 are grounded in the context, score = 8/10 = 0.8 (20% hallucination). Note: whether you include ambiguous ("I don't know") claims in the denominator can change the score; you can adjust the truth-extraction limit and whether to count ambiguous claims.
testCases.expectedOutput:
Faithfulness measures how well a response stays grounded in the retrieved context, without adding extra unsupported claims.  
Its score is computed as:

**faithfulness = grounded claims / total claims**

In the example, if **7 out of 9** claims are grounded, the faithfulness score is **7/9**.

testCases.actualOutput: Because that reject step is configured to run "always." Even when the promotion job fails or other jobs are skipped, the always-run setting forces the reject job to execute so it can remove the challenger tag. This is intentional cleanup: when promotion fails you must clear the challenger tag so the next run will correctly be the challenger (and you don’t leave a stale challenger). Using separate jobs (to avoid re-running expensive experiment-tracking steps) makes this independent cleanup necessary.

testCases.input: What are retriever failures, plus metrics and tunable params for each?
testCases.actualOutput:
Retriever failures (3), metric for each, and tunable parameters you can change:

1) Coverage / completeness
- Failure: retriever does not fetch enough of the relevant context.
- Metric: contextual recall.
- Tunable params: chunk size, chunk overlap, TopK (how many chunks you retrieve), embedding model (encoding quality).
- Tuning guidance from context: if recall is low → increase chunk size (retrieve more information).

2) Relevancy of retrieved results
- Failure: retrieved chunks are not relevant to the query.
- Metric: contextual relevancy.
- Tunable params: chunk size, chunk overlap, TopK, embedding model.
- Tuning guidance from context: if relevancy is low → decrease chunk size.

3) Ranking / order of results
- Failure: relevant items are returned in wrong order.
- Metric: precision (ranking/order).
- Tunable params: TopK, embedding model, and add or tune a reranker (cross‑encoder) that re-scores results (retriever is a bi-encoder; reranker is a separate transformer/cross-encoder).
- Note from context: precision is mainly used to evaluate ranking/reranker; in production you often test the retriever, so precision may be less relevant unless you use a reranker.
testCases.expectedOutput:
Retriever failures fall into 3 main types:

1. **Coverage / completeness failure**  
   - Problem: the retriever isn’t bringing enough of the total relevant context.  
   - Metric: **Contextual recall**  
   - Tunable params: **embedding model**, **top-k**, **chunk size**

2. **Relevancy / signal-to-noise failure**  
   - Problem: retrieved chunks are not relevant enough to the query.  
   - Metric: **Contextual relevancy**  
   - Tunable params: **top-k**, **chunk size**, **chunk overlap**, and also the **embedding model**

3. **Ranking / order failure**  
   - Problem: relevant chunks are retrieved, but their order is wrong.  
   - Metric: **Precision**  
   - Tunable params: mainly the **reranker** and its settings

In short:  
- **Recall issues** → tune retrieval coverage settings  
- **Relevancy issues** → reduce noise via top-k, chunk size, overlap  
- **Precision/ranking issues** → improve or tune the reranker

- Core duty (both EC2 and ASG): the CodeDeploy agent continuously polls the CodeDeploy service. When a new deployment appears it is triggered, reads the app spec (appspec.yml / apps.yaml) and runs the scripts there (install Docker/CLI, validate, start the app). In short: the agent runs the actual commands on the machine—what you would otherwise run manually.

- On standalone EC2 instances: the agent is already on the instance and simply watches for deployments and executes the app spec steps on that single instance.

- On Auto Scaling Group (ASG) instances: the agent’s work is the same on each instance (poll, detect deployment, run app spec). The difference is that instances are created automatically from a launch template (with the agent preinstalled). As the ASG scales or a new deployment runs across the group, each launched/targeted instance’s agent will perform the same scripts so the new version gets deployed across the ASG.

- Summary: duties do not change—the agent always polls and executes the app spec. The environment differs: EC2 is a fixed machine you manage; ASG adds automatic instance creation (via the launch template and desired capacity) so agents run on dynamically created instances as part of the group.
testCases.expectedOutput:
On EC2 or in an Auto Scaling Group, the CodeDeploy agent does the same core job: it polls CodeDeploy for a new deployment and, when triggered, runs the scripts in `appspec.yml` on the instance.

- **On EC2:** the agent runs on that single machine and executes the deployment commands there.
- **On ASG:** the agent runs on each instance in the group, so CodeDeploy can deploy across multiple instances automatically.

So the difference is mainly **scope**: EC2 = one machine, ASG = multiple managed instances.

testCases.input: How did concurrency plus parallel contextual compression reduce AWS retrieval latency from 40–50s to ~10s?
testCases.actualOutput:
Because you stopped doing compression and retrieval sequentially and made them concurrent across chunks. Instead of processing each chunk one after another (which summed to 40–50s), you send all chunks and compress them in parallel. That means total time becomes roughly the time of the slowest chunk (the “weakest link”) — which in your traces is about 11.69s — rather than the sum of all chunk times. Introducing concurrency for contextual compression therefore cut the retrieval+compression step down to ~10s. 

Also note from your context: contextual compression itself adds an extra LLM call (which can multiply per-chunk latency), but because those calls run in parallel the overall latency is still much lower. Streaming generation on the frontend further hides remaining generation latency.
testCases.expectedOutput: By running the retrieval and contextual compression steps in parallel instead of sequentially. This concurrency reduced the retrieval phase from about 40–50 seconds to around 10 seconds, cutting overall latency by more than 50% in some cases.

testCases.name: test_case_23
testCases.input: Compare Prometheus static configs vs EC2 service discovery for ASG targets in YAML; explain why static fails.
testCases.actualOutput:
- Static configs
  - You list the full addresses (IP or URL) of every scrape target in prometheus.yml (static_configs).
  - Works only when endpoints are fixed and known up front.
  - Fails for ASG targets because instances are dynamic: new instances are created and others are terminated, their IPs change, and you cannot keep the static list up to date. Because traffic is handled by a load balancer and instances come and go, the static addresses will often be unavailable.

- EC2 service discovery (SDB)
  - Instead of hardcoding addresses you add an ec2 service discovery block in prometheus.yml.
  - Prometheus calls the EC2 describe instances API to discover instances automatically (by tags, metadata, availability zone, IP, etc.).
  - It uses private IPs by default (you can change to public IP via relabeling).
  - Requires the Prometheus EC2 instance to have an IAM role/policy allowing DescribeInstances so the metadata is exposed.
  - This lets Prometheus dynamically track ASG targets as they appear and disappear and scrape their metrics automatically.

- Why static fails and SDB succeeds
  - Static fails because ASG instances are ephemeral and IPs/endpoints are not constant.
  - EC2 service discovery succeeds because it discovers targets via instance metadata/tags at runtime, keeping the scrape target list up to date without manual changes.

testCases.input: How do hashed chunk IDs compare with plain chunks in preventing vector-store duplicates?
testCases.actualOutput:
Hashed/unique chunk IDs let you detect and skip chunks that are already stored. In the pipeline described you create a unique ID (e.g., filename::chunkIndex), store it with the chunk metadata, ask the vector store whether those candidate IDs exist, and if the existing hash equals the new hash you skip embedding; otherwise you embed and add. That prevents duplicate entries and saves API calls.

Plain chunks (no unique IDs/hashes) give you no reliable way to detect existing content, so you risk re-embedding and creating duplicate entries in the vector store.
